cards.text: This one's a song of David, Israel's king, written for the choirmaster with stringed instruments. David opens by crying out, asking God to hear his prayer. No small talk, no 'hey, how you been,' just STRAIGHT to it.

cards.question: David is crying out to God. Where does he say he's calling from?

answers.text: The other side of the Jordan

cards.text: The ends of the earth, friend, and David calls from there whenever his heart is faint. Me? I spent years in the back of a junk drawer yelling 'HELLO?' and the only thing that answered was a twist tie.

cards.question: David calls out to God whenever his heart is faint. Where does he ask God to lead him?

answers.text: To the rock higher than himself
To his father's house in Bethlehem

cards.text: A rock HIGHER than him, baker, not a pebble and not a step stool. I live my whole life on a little gold base, so trust me, I respect anybody asking for something taller.

cards.question: David gives his reason for turning to God. He says God has already been his ___.

cards.text: A refuge and a tower of strength against the enemy. That's not a pep talk, friend, that's a building you can run INTO.

cards.question: David asks to dwell in God's tent for one night, just until the trouble passes.

cards.text: Not one night, baker. FOREVER. David wants to live in God's tent and take refuge in the shelter of His wings.

cards.question: David asks to live in God's tent forever, and the reason he gives is that God has heard his vows.
David says God has given him the inheritance reserved for those who ___ His name.

cards.text: RESERVED, baker, like a seat with your name already taped to it. Then the prayer turns to the king.

cards.question: Now the prayer is for the king. What does it ask God to do for him?

answers.text: Increase the days of his life

cards.text: And may his years span many generations, baker. That's not 'happy birthday,' that's 'have ALL the birthdays.'

cards.question: The prayer asks for the king to rule far away from God's presence.
The prayer asks God to appoint something to guard the king. What is it?

answers.text: A thousand of Israel's mighty warriors

cards.text: Loving devotion and faithfulness on guard duty. Two bodyguards, friend, and neither one EVER clocks out.

cards.question: To close, David says he will ever ___ praise to God's name and fulfill his ___ day by day.

cards.text: Day by day, baker. I bet that's one alarm David never hits snooze on.

findings.problem: Asks the baker to guess a detail of the psalm's wording (where David calls from) with nothing on card 1 to reason from. This matches the Psalm 23 bad example, where the baker guesses a detail instead of reasoning about the movement or meaning.

rule.text: Ask about the movement and the meaning: what changes, what the picture is, why the speaker says what he says.

findings.problem: The joke compares David's plea to be led to a rock higher than himself with Papa Dorin standing on a 'little gold base.' The base raises him up, so the height comparison doesn't click and needs explaining. It also doesn't share the core action, which is being led to safety. Calling the base 'little' adds a new detail to his look.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: The true or false statement relies on two verses: living in God's tent forever (61:4) and God hearing his vows (61:5). The card cites only Psalm 61:5. It should cite Psalm 61:4-5.

rule.text: A choice card cites only the verses of its right answer.

findings.problem: The blank asks the baker to supply the exact wording of the line ('those who ___ His name'), which nothing earlier sets up. Only the weak wrong answers make it solvable, not reasoning about the meaning.

rule.text: The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: The wrong answers 'forget' and 'deny' are silly in context. An inheritance reserved for those who forget or deny God's name doesn't fit a prayer of trust, so 'fear' stands out as the only fitting answer.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.
